title: Aubergine Parmigiana
subtitle: Layered fried aubergine with tomato sauce and melted cheese
excerpt: Aubergine parmigiana is sliced aubergine, fried until golden, layered with tomato sauce and mozzarella, and baked until bubbling and browned at the edges. It's the vegetarian original that inspired the chicken and veal versions in Italian-American cooking, and it's the best of the three.
sourceNotes: Melanzane alla parmigiana is a dish with roots in Sicilian and southern Italian cooking, pre-dating the American veal and chicken versions. The exact origin is debated, but it is well documented in Neapolitan and Sicilian cooking traditions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze assembled and baked. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat at 180°C covered for 20 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble a day ahead and refrigerate before baking. Add ten minutes to the covered bake time if going in cold.

content.text: Aubergine parmigiana is layers of fried aubergine slices, tomato sauce, and melted mozzarella baked together until the whole thing is set and bronzed on top. The salting step is optional but recommended: it draws out moisture so the slices fry rather than steam. The dish needs a rest before cutting, otherwise the layers slide apart.

Lay the sliced aubergine on a rack or plate lined with kitchen paper, salt generously, and leave for 30 minutes. Pat dry before frying. The slices will fry faster and absorb less oil. If you're short of time, skip the salting and fry in smaller batches with a little more heat.
Salt, rinse, and fry the aubergine
Arrange the {{aubergine}} slices on a rack or plate. Sprinkle generously with {{sea-salt-flakes}} and leave for 30 minutes. Rinse and pat dry with kitchen paper.

Heat a generous amount of {{olive-oil}} in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the aubergine slices in batches, two to three minutes per side, until golden and soft. Lay on kitchen paper to drain. Add more oil between batches as needed: aubergine absorbs a lot.

Warm {{olive-oil}} in a saucepan. Add {{garlic}} and cook gently for one minute. Add the {{tinned-tomatoes}}, season with salt, and simmer for 15 minutes until slightly reduced. Remove from the heat and stir in half the {{basil}}.

Heat the oven to 190°C (fan 170°C / gas mark 5). Spread a thin layer of tomato sauce over the base of a 23 cm baking dish. Add a layer of fried {{aubergine}} slices, overlapping slightly. Spoon over more sauce, scatter some {{mozzarella}}, and sprinkle with {{parmesan}}. Add a few {{basil}} leaves.
Repeat the layers until the dish is full, ending with sauce and a generous scattering of both cheeses. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the top is golden and bubbling at the edges.
Rest for at least 15 minutes before cutting. This allows the layers to settle and the dish to hold its shape when served.

items.symptom: The aubergine is oily and greasy
items.cause: Fried at too low a temperature, or not dried properly after salting.
items.fix: The oil must be hot enough that the aubergine sizzles on contact. Drain fried slices on kitchen paper. Salting and patting dry before frying significantly reduces oil absorption.

items.symptom: The dish is watery after baking
items.cause: Mozzarella releases liquid as it melts, and unsalted aubergine also weeps.
items.fix: Salt and dry the aubergine before frying. Drain the mozzarella on kitchen paper for 20 minutes before using. If the dish looks very wet, drain off the excess liquid and return to the oven for ten more minutes.

items.symptom: The layers slide apart when cut
items.cause: Cut before the dish had time to set.
items.fix: The 15-minute rest is not optional. The sauce and melted cheese need time to firm up. For cleaner slices, refrigerate for an hour and reheat portions individually.

items.cause: Older or very large aubergines can be bitter.
items.fix: Salting and rinsing removes some of the bitter compounds. Use firm, shiny aubergines with no wrinkled skin: these are fresher and milder.

content.text: Melanzane alla parmigiana is from southern Italy and Sicily, where aubergines have been grown since the Arab influence in the medieval period. Parma is not the origin. The name most likely comes from palmigiana, meaning slatted shutter, from the overlapping slices. The dish is the ancestor of every veal and chicken parmigiana in Italian-American cooking. Serve with bread and a green salad.
